**Jeremy Strong**(born December 25, 1978) is an American actor.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-1) Known for his intense [method acting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Method_acting "Method acting") style in roles across both stage and screen,[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-3) he has received [accolades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_awards_and_nominations_received_by_Jeremy_Strong "List of awards and nominations received by Jeremy Strong") including a [Tony Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Award "Tony Award"), a [Primetime Emmy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primetime_Emmy_Award "Primetime Emmy Award"), and a [Golden Globe Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globe_Award "Golden Globe Award") as well as nominations for an [Academy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award "Academy Award") and a [BAFTA Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAFTA_Award "BAFTA Award"). In 2022, Strong was featured on _[Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time\_(magazine) "Time (magazine)")_'s list of the [100 most influential people in the world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_100 "Time 100").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-4)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-5)

A graduate of [Yale University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_University "Yale University"), Strong studied acting at the[Royal Academy of Dramatic Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Academy_of_Dramatic_Art "Royal Academy of Dramatic Art")in London and the[Steppenwolf Theatre Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steppenwolf_Theatre_Company "Steppenwolf Theatre Company")in Chicago. His film debut came that same year with the comedy _[Humboldt County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humboldt\_County\_(film) "Humboldt County (film)")_, and he played small roles in the films _[Lincoln](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lincoln\_(film) "Lincoln (film)")_ (2012), _[Zero Dark Thirty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zero\_Dark\_Thirty "Zero Dark Thirty")_ (2012), _[Parkland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parkland\_(film) "Parkland (film)")_ (2013), and _[The Big Short](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Big\_Short\_(film) "The Big Short (film)")_ (2015). Strong's [breakthrough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breakthrough_role "Breakthrough role") was his portrayal of [Kendall Roy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kendall_Roy "Kendall Roy") in the [HBO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HBO "HBO") drama series _[Succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Succession\_(TV\_series) "Succession (TV series)")_ (2018–2023), winning the [Primetime Emmy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primetime_Emmy_Award_for_Outstanding_Lead_Actor_in_a_Drama_Series "Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Lead Actor in a Drama Series") and the [Golden Globe Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globe_Award_for_Best_Actor_%E2%80%93_Television_Series_Drama "Golden Globe Award for Best Actor – Television Series Drama") for Best Actor in a Drama Series.

Strong acted in the films _[The Gentlemen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Gentlemen\_(2019\_film) "The Gentlemen (2019 film)")_ (2019), _[The Trial of the Chicago 7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Trial\_of\_the\_Chicago\_7 "The Trial of the Chicago 7")_ (2020), and _[Armageddon Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armageddon\_Time "Armageddon Time")_ (2022). For his portrayal of [Roy Cohn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_Cohn "Roy Cohn") in the biographical drama _[The Apprentice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Apprentice\_(2024\_film) "The Apprentice (2024 film)")_ (2024) he earned Best Supporting Actor nominations for the [Academy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Supporting_Actor "Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor"), [Actor Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Actor_Award_for_Outstanding_Performance_by_a_Male_Actor_in_a_Supporting_Role "Actor Award for Outstanding Performance by a Male Actor in a Supporting Role"), [BAFTA Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAFTA_Award_for_Best_Actor_in_a_Supporting_Role "BAFTA Award for Best Actor in a Supporting Role"), and [Golden Globe Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globe_Award_for_Best_Supporting_Actor_%E2%80%93_Motion_Picture "Golden Globe Award for Best Supporting Actor – Motion Picture"). In 2025, he portrayed music producer [Jon Landau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jon_Landau "Jon Landau") in the musical biopic _[Springsteen: Deliver Me from Nowhere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Springsteen:\_Deliver\_Me\_from\_Nowhere "Springsteen: Deliver Me from Nowhere")_.

On stage, Strong made his [off-Broadway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Off-Broadway "Off-Broadway") debut in the [John Patrick Shanley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Patrick_Shanley "John Patrick Shanley") play _[Defiance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defiance\_(play) "Defiance (play)")_ in 2006, with his [Broadway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadway_theatre "Broadway theatre") debut portrayed the role of [Richard Rich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Rich,_1st_Baron_Rich "Richard Rich, 1st Baron Rich") in the revival of _[A Man for All Seasons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Man\_for\_All\_Seasons\_(play) "A Man for All Seasons (play)")_ in 2008. He returned to Broadway playing a conscientious doctor in a small town in the revival of the [Henrik Ibsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henrik_Ibsen "Henrik Ibsen") play _[An Enemy of the People](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An\_Enemy\_of\_the\_People "An Enemy of the People")_ in 2024, earning a [Tony Award for Best Actor in a Play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Award_for_Best_Actor_in_a_Play "Tony Award for Best Actor in a Play").

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jeremy_Strong&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Strong was born on 25 December 1978 in [Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston "Boston"), Massachusetts, to Maureen and David Strong. His mother is of Irish descent, and his father's family is [Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jews "Jews"), originally from Russia; his paternal grandfather worked as a plumber in [Queens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queens "Queens"), New York City.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-6)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-7)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-8) His mother worked as a hospice nurse, and his father worked in [juvenile jails](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Youth_detention_center "Youth detention center").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-New_Yorker_profile-2) He lived in a "rough neighborhood" in the [Jamaica Plain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamaica_Plain "Jamaica Plain") area of Boston, a place he often regarded as "somewhere I just wanted to get out of." His family was working class. Since his parents could not afford to go on vacations outside the Boston area, they put a canoe on cinder blocks in the family's backyard; Strong and his brothers would often sit in it and pretend to take trips.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-New_Yorker_profile-2) His parents had a tumultuous relationship throughout his childhood and eventually divorced.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-CBS-9)

When Strong was 10, his parents moved the family to the suburb of [Sudbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sudbury,_Massachusetts "Sudbury, Massachusetts"),[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-gq2019-10) for better schools. Strong recalled Sudbury as "a kind of country-club town where we didn't belong to the country club". His interest in acting began there, as he became involved with a children's theater group and performing in musicals. Among his costars in the children's theater group was [Chris Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Evans_(actor) "Chris Evans (actor)")' older sister; Evans remembers being impressed by Strong's performances. Later, Evans and Strong acted with each other in a high school production of _[A Midsummer Night's Dream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Midsummer\_Night's\_Dream "A Midsummer Night's Dream")_.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-New_Yorker_profile-2)

Strong particularly idolized actors [Daniel Day-Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Day-Lewis "Daniel Day-Lewis"), [Al Pacino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Pacino "Al Pacino"), and [Dustin Hoffman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dustin_Hoffman "Dustin Hoffman")—all famous for the lengths they went to preparing for roles—putting posters of their films on his bedroom wall and avidly following news of their careers as well as reading every interview they gave. When the [1996 film adaptation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Crucible_(1996_film) "The Crucible (1996 film)") of [Arthur Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Miller "Arthur Miller")'s _[The Crucible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Crucible "The Crucible")_, starring Day-Lewis, was filmed near Boston, Strong got a job on the film's greenery crew, at one point holding up a branch outside a window during the filming of a scene. Strong worked on the sound crew for _[Amistad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amistad\_(film) "Amistad (film)")_, holding a [boom mike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boom_mike "Boom mike") over [Anthony Hopkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Hopkins "Anthony Hopkins") as he made a speech, and he helped to edit Pacino's directorial debut _[Looking for Richard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Looking\_for\_Richard "Looking for Richard")_.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-New_Yorker_profile-2)

After high school, Strong applied to colleges with a letter of recommendation from [DreamWorks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DreamWorks_Pictures "DreamWorks Pictures"), which had made _Amistad_. He was accepted at [Yale University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_University "Yale University") and granted a scholarship, intending to study drama.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-nytimes2015-11) On his first day in class, he found the professor's discussions of [Konstantin Stanislavski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Konstantin_Stanislavski "Konstantin Stanislavski") and accompanying blackboard illustrations so alienating that he decided immediately to change his major to English.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-New_Yorker_profile-2)

Strong continued to act and starred in a number of plays at Yale, all of them produced through the student-run [Yale Dramatic Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_Dramatic_Association "Yale Dramatic Association"), known as Dramat. The plays were all ones that Pacino had performed, such as _[American Buffalo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American\_Buffalo\_(play) "American Buffalo (play)")_, _[The Indian Wants the Bronx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Indian\_Wants\_the\_Bronx "The Indian Wants the Bronx")_, and _[Hughie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hughie "Hughie")_. Strong arranged an offstage visit from Pacino, which did not go down well with other members of Dramat, because it was budgeted so extravagantly that it nearly bankrupted their organization. Despite claiming not to remember the cost overruns, Strong admitted to being a "rogue agent" in planning the event. During one summer at Yale, Strong received an internship with Hoffman's production company. He also studied at the [Royal Academy of Dramatic Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Academy_of_Dramatic_Art "Royal Academy of Dramatic Art") in London and the [Steppenwolf Theatre Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steppenwolf_Theatre_Company "Steppenwolf Theatre Company") in Chicago.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-New_Yorker_profile-2)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jeremy_Strong&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

### 2001–2008: Early years on stage

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jeremy_Strong&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 2001–2008: Early years on stage")]

After Yale, Strong moved to New York in 2001. He lived in a small apartment in [SoHo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SoHo,_Manhattan "SoHo, Manhattan"), above a restaurant where he waited tables. Strong described it as a state of "gilded squalor" (in the words of [Francis Bacon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Bacon_(artist) "Francis Bacon (artist)")), with little but his bed, books, and a closet with expensive clothing. When not working, he persuaded local [FedEx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FedEx "FedEx") offices to give him some free envelopes in which he put headshots and recordings of himself performing monologues to distribute to talent agencies. For almost a year, he got no calls for auditions. In an attempt to get representation, Strong contacted his former high school classmate Evans, who had become successful after _[Not Another Teen Movie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Not\_Another\_Teen\_Movie "Not Another Teen Movie")_. Evans set up a meeting between Strong and his agent at [Creative Artists Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creative_Artists_Agency "Creative Artists Agency"), who chose not to sign Strong.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-New_Yorker_profile-2)

The following summer, Strong got a spot in the summer company at the [Williamstown Theatre Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Williamstown_Theatre_Festival "Williamstown Theatre Festival") in western Massachusetts. Strong continued to work offstage in theater and film. In 2003, his position as an assistant at an independent film production company led to his service as Day-Lewis's personal assistant on _[The Ballad of Jack and Rose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Ballad\_of\_Jack\_and\_Rose "The Ballad of Jack and Rose")_, released two years later. On set, he was so devoted to attending to Day-Lewis, who lived apart from his family during the shoot, that crew members nicknamed him [Cletus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_recurring_The_Simpsons_characters#Cletus_Spuckler "List of recurring The Simpsons characters") after [the character from _The Simpsons_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_recurring_The_Simpsons_characters "List of recurring The Simpsons characters"), for his focus on menial tasks. Strong has stated that at the end of the shoot, Day-Lewis wrote him a note "that contains many of what have become my most deeply held precepts and beliefs about this work." He has not publicized the contents of the note out of respect for Day-Lewis.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-New_Yorker_profile-2)

Strong returned to Williamstown in 2004 when he was cast with [Jessica Chastain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessica_Chastain "Jessica Chastain"), [Chris Messina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Messina "Chris Messina"), and [Michelle Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Williams_(actress) "Michelle Williams (actress)") in _[The Cherry Orchard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Cherry\_Orchard "The Cherry Orchard")_. He became friends with all three actors, and for intermittent periods in the late 2000s, he lived in the basement of Williams' townhouse in the Brooklyn neighborhood of [Boerum Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boerum_Hill "Boerum Hill") when he could not afford his own apartment.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-New_Yorker_profile-2)

During the mid-2000s, he worked as a typist for playwright [Wendy Wasserstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wendy_Wasserstein "Wendy Wasserstein"). At night, he performed the role of an alcoholic Irishman in a one-man [Conor McPherson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conor_McPherson "Conor McPherson") play in a small bar in Midtown Manhattan. After Wasserstein discovered how much time Strong was spending observing her building's Irish doorman for the part, she considered writing a play based on Strong and the doorman but was unable to proceed with it before her death in 2006.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-New_Yorker_profile-2)[Frank Rich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Rich "Frank Rich"), one of Wasserstein's close friends, said Strong was "her assistant, slash—to some extent—caregiver."[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-Ringer-12)

By that time, Strong had begun getting [off-Broadway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Off-Broadway "Off-Broadway") roles. He took part in Marine weapons training at [Camp Lejeune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_Corps_Base_Camp_Lejeune "Marine Corps Base Camp Lejeune") to prepare for his role as a marine in the [John Patrick Shanley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Patrick_Shanley "John Patrick Shanley") play _[Defiance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defiance\_(play) "Defiance (play)")_ (2005). David Rooney described Strong's character as a "a distraught, uneducated soldier from the small-town South". Rooney described his performance as "intense" noting, "while [the] dramaturgical shortcomings hamper the actors...Strong has emotional impact in his single scene."[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-13) Strong immersed himself in early [17th-century](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/17th-century "17th-century")[Dutch philosophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_philosophy "Dutch philosophy") to play a young [Baruch Spinoza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baruch_Spinoza "Baruch Spinoza") in [David Ives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Ives "David Ives")'s _[New Jerusalem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New\_Jerusalem\_(play) "New Jerusalem (play)")_ in 2008. Also in 2008, Strong was asked to [understudy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Understudy "Understudy") with six hours' notice for an actor who had a family emergency; by the next night, he had memorized all the character's lines. He received favorable notice for this performance, and he was able to sign with an agent.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-New_Yorker_profile-2)

### 2009–2023: Film roles and _Succession_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jeremy_Strong&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 2009–2023: Film roles and Succession")]

Later in 2008, he made his [Broadway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadway_theatre "Broadway theatre") debut in _[A Man for All Seasons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Man\_for\_All\_Seasons\_(play) "A Man for All Seasons (play)")_ at the [American Airlines Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Airlines_Theatre "American Airlines Theatre").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-nytimes2015-11) Strong portrayed [Richard Rich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Rich,_1st_Baron_Rich "Richard Rich, 1st Baron Rich") opposite [Frank Langella](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Langella "Frank Langella") as [Thomas More](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_More "Thomas More"). [Ben Brantley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Brantley "Ben Brantley") of _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_ described Strong as a "talented" actor portraying the "ambitious moral-chameleon".[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-14) He was chosen as the 2008/2009 Leonore Annenberg Fellow by [Lincoln Center Theater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lincoln_Center_Theater "Lincoln Center Theater") and nominated for the [Lucille Lortel Award for Outstanding Lead Actor in a Play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucille_Lortel_Award_for_Outstanding_Lead_Actor_in_a_Play?action=edit&redlink=1 "Lucille Lortel Award for Outstanding Lead Actor in a Play (page does not exist)") twice within a three-year period.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-Lucille_2008-15)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-Lortel_2011-16) Strong's _Defiance_ role helped him secure his first film role in _[Humboldt County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humboldt\_County\_(film) "Humboldt County (film)")_.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-gq2019-10) He played [Abraham Lincoln](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Lincoln "Abraham Lincoln")'s secretary [John George Nicolay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_George_Nicolay "John George Nicolay"), acting opposite Day-Lewis in [Steven Spielberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Spielberg "Steven Spielberg")'s historical drama _[Lincoln](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lincoln\_(film) "Lincoln (film)")_ (2012).

He went on to play a [CIA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CIA "CIA") analyst in [Kathryn Bigelow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathryn_Bigelow "Kathryn Bigelow")'s historical drama _[Zero Dark Thirty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zero\_Dark\_Thirty "Zero Dark Thirty")_ (2012) opposite Chastain, [Lee Harvey Oswald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Harvey_Oswald "Lee Harvey Oswald") in political drama _[Parkland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parkland\_(film) "Parkland (film)")_ (2013), [James Reeb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Reeb "James Reeb") in [Ava DuVernay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ava_DuVernay "Ava DuVernay")'s civil rights drama _[Selma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selma\_(film) "Selma (film)")_ (2014), a mentally-disabled person in legal drama _[The Judge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Judge\_(2014\_film) "The Judge (2014 film)")_ (2014), and a real estate developer in [Aaron Sorkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Sorkin "Aaron Sorkin")'s drama _[Molly's Game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molly's\_Game "Molly's Game")_ (2017), reuniting with Chastain again.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-17) Strong was set to play a leading role in a major film for the first time in Bigelow's period crime drama _[Detroit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detroit\_(film) "Detroit (film)")_ (2017) as a soldier and practiced his marksmanship in preparation, but he was fired from the film after the first day of shooting because, according to Bigelow, "the character wasn't working in the story." Strong later persuaded her to give him another part in the film.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-New_Yorker_profile-2)

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/75/Jeremy_Strong_2014.jpg/250px-Jeremy_Strong_2014.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jeremy_Strong_2014.jpg)

Strong in 2014

Strong's role in the 2015 [Adam McKay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam_McKay "Adam McKay") film _[The Big Short](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Big\_Short\_(film) "The Big Short (film)")_ led McKay to offer him a part in the TV series _[Succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Succession\_(TV\_series) "Succession (TV series)")_.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-gq2019-10)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-:0-18) He initially was interested in playing [Roman Roy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Succession_characters#Roman_Roy "List of Succession characters"), the family's wisecracking youngest son, but after the part was given to [Kieran Culkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kieran_Culkin "Kieran Culkin"), Strong auditioned for the part of the middle son, [Kendall Roy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kendall_Roy "Kendall Roy"). The role was a career breakthrough for him; Strong's performance in the role has received universal acclaim from critics, and his performance won him a [Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Lead Actor in a Drama Series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primetime_Emmy_Award_for_Outstanding_Lead_Actor_in_a_Drama_Series "Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Lead Actor in a Drama Series") in [2020](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/72nd_Primetime_Emmy_Awards "72nd Primetime Emmy Awards").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-19)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-New_Yorker_profile-2) He also received the [Golden Globe Award for Best Actor – Television Series Drama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globe_Award_for_Best_Actor_%E2%80%93_Television_Series_Drama "Golden Globe Award for Best Actor – Television Series Drama")[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-20) and an [Actor Award for Outstanding Performance by an Ensemble in a Drama Series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Actor_Award_for_Outstanding_Performance_by_an_Ensemble_in_a_Drama_Series "Actor Award for Outstanding Performance by an Ensemble in a Drama Series"). _[TVLine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TVLine "TVLine")_ named Strong "Performer of the Year" in 2021 for his work on _Succession_, writing, "For three seasons now, Strong has been carefully crafting a portrait of a little boy lost, a man who knows how to play the corporate hero but doesn't know how to be OK with himself.... _Succession_ remains one of the best shows on television in large part because Strong's central performance is so complex and so fascinating."[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-21)

Strong appeared in [Guy Ritchie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guy_Ritchie "Guy Ritchie")'s action comedy _[The Gentlemen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Gentlemen\_(2019\_film) "The Gentlemen (2019 film)")_ (2019), a film that he did not want to discuss on the record with _The New Yorker_.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-New_Yorker_profile-2) In 2020, he reunited with Sorkin playing a central role as anti-war activist [Jerry Rubin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerry_Rubin "Jerry Rubin"), part of the [Chicago Seven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Seven "Chicago Seven"), in the Sorkin's directed [Netflix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netflix "Netflix") drama _[The Trial of the Chicago 7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Trial\_of\_the\_Chicago\_7 "The Trial of the Chicago 7")_ (2020). Rooney of _[The Hollywood Reporter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Hollywood\_Reporter "The Hollywood Reporter")_ wrote "Strong gives Jerry a touching puppy-dog innocence and vulnerability".[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-22) For his performance he was nominated for an [Actor Award for Outstanding Performance by a Cast in a Motion Picture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Actor_Award_for_Outstanding_Performance_by_a_Cast_in_a_Motion_Picture "Actor Award for Outstanding Performance by a Cast in a Motion Picture").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-23) The film received critical acclaim as well as six nominations in the [93rd Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/93rd_Academy_Awards "93rd Academy Awards").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-24)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-25) He acted in the [James Gray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gray_(director) "James Gray (director)")[coming-of-age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coming-of-age "Coming-of-age") drama _[Armageddon Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armageddon\_Time "Armageddon Time")_ (2022) alongside [Anne Hathaway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anne_Hathaway "Anne Hathaway") and Hopkins. The film had its world premiere at the [2022 Cannes Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Cannes_Film_Festival "2022 Cannes Film Festival").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-26)[Justin Chang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justin_Chang "Justin Chang") of _[NPR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NPR "NPR")_ wrote, "Strong is terrific — and very un-[Kendall Roy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kendall_Roy "Kendall Roy")-like — as Paul's father, a plumber with a big heart and a fierce temper".[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-27)

## Acting philosophy and technique

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jeremy_Strong&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Acting philosophy and technique")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cb/Jeremy_Strong_%2847653791142%29_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Jeremy_Strong_%2847653791142%29_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jeremy_Strong_(47653791142)_(cropped).jpg)

Strong in 2019

Strong prepares intensely for his roles, often to replicate some aspect of the character whether or not it is prominent in his portrayal. He has stated, "I think you have to go through whatever the ordeal is that the character has to go through". For _The Judge_, where he played the main character's developmentally disabled younger brother, he spent time with an autistic man as Hoffman had for _[Rain Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rain\_Man "Rain Man")_, and he requested personalized props for the character not mentioned in the script. "All I know is, he [crosses the Rubicon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossing_the_Rubicon "Crossing the Rubicon")", said costar [Robert Downey Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Downey_Jr. "Robert Downey Jr.").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-New_Yorker_profile-2) For _The Big Short_, Strong followed his real life counterpart Vincent Daniel, and observed his mannerisms, which included constantly chewing gum, something Strong did in all his scenes.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-New_York_Times-46) In preparation for his _Succession_ audition for Kendall Roy, he read [Michael Wolff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Wolff_(journalist) "Michael Wolff (journalist)")'s biography of media mogul [Rupert Murdoch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupert_Murdoch "Rupert Murdoch") and [his family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murdoch_family "Murdoch family"), which mentions that Murdoch's son [James](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Murdoch "James Murdoch") is known for lacing his shoes very tightly; Strong thus did the same for the audition, believing that it expressed the character's "inner tensile strength".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-New_Yorker_profile-2)

Strong's devotion to his craft occasionally has led to personal injury. In the first season _Succession_ episode "[Which Side Are You On?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Which_Side_Are_You_On%3F_(Succession) "Which Side Are You On? (Succession)")", his character had to run a considerable distance to be present at a board meeting after his limousine gets stuck in traffic. Because Strong wanted to be genuinely sweaty and breathless in every take, he ran as fast and far as he could in [Tom Ford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Ford "Tom Ford") dress shoes and fractured his foot. Two seasons later, he jumped off a 5-foot-high (1.5 m) platform, wearing [Gucci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gucci "Gucci") shoes while filming the episode "[Too Much Birthday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Too_Much_Birthday "Too Much Birthday")",[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-47) impacting his tibia and femur and requiring a leg brace. The take ultimately was not used.

Strong seldom rehearses, saying he wants "every scene to feel like I'm encountering a bear in the woods", an approach he admits may not be popular with his costars. On _The Trial of the Chicago 7_, Strong asked to be sprayed with [tear gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tear_gas "Tear gas"). Director Sorkin stated "I don't like saying no to Jeremy... But there were 200 people in that scene and another seventy on the crew, so I declined to spray them with poison gas".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-New_Yorker_profile-2)

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6b/Jeremy_Strong_at_the_2025_Cannes_Film_Festival_28.jpg/250px-Jeremy_Strong_at_the_2025_Cannes_Film_Festival_28.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jeremy_Strong_at_the_2025_Cannes_Film_Festival_28.jpg)

Strong at the [Cannes Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannes_Film_Festival "Cannes Film Festival") in 2025

On _Succession_, Strong intentionally deepened his alienation from the rest of the cast by timing his visits to the makeup trailer to be the only one there at the time. His costar Culkin described Strong as being in "a bubble" before shoots: "It's hard for me to actually describe his process because I don't really see it".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-New_Yorker_profile-2) Culkin has stated that Strong's methods are not intrusive to his own process.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-48)[Matthew Macfadyen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matthew_Macfadyen "Matthew Macfadyen") described Strong's techniques as "not the main event... That's not to say that's wrong. That's just not useful".[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-49)[Brian Cox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Cox_(actor) "Brian Cox (actor)"), who portrayed Strong's character's father on the show, expressed his concerns that Strong's intense approach to acting may lead to early burnout. However, he added that Strong's performance "is always extraordinary and excellent".[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-50) During the shooting of _The Big Short_, Strong similarly reduced the interactions with his cast mates, although he admitted to having a good time, he also found it to be "distracting" and "depleting," recalling, "These guys can all be in a comedy, but I need to feel like I’m in a global warming catastrophe documentary."[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-New_York_Times-46)

Similar to [method acting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Method_acting "Method acting"), Strong uses the term "identity diffusion" to describe his technique because he does not draw on his own life experience. "If I have any method at all, it is simply this: to clear away anything—anything—that is not the character and the circumstances of the scene... And usually that means clearing away almost everything around and inside you, so that you can be a more complete vessel for the work at hand". He quoted jazz pianist [Keith Jarrett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett "Keith Jarrett") to explain his approach to acting: "I connect every music-making experience I have, including every day here in the studio, with a great power, and if I do not surrender to it nothing happens".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-New_Yorker_profile-2) Strong admits the intensity he brings to his work might cause him problems, and he has stated "I don't know if I even believe in balance... I believe in extremity". His wife has stated that "He does a really good job of maintaining what he's doing but also creating a space for the family and a normal life".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-New_Yorker_profile-2)

Strong has noted a preference for films based on actual events, such as _Selma_, _Detroit_, and _The Trial of the Chicago 7_, saying he "never wanted anything more than to be part of telling stories that feel meaningful, films about social justice in particular."[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-51)

Along with Day-Lewis, Hoffman, and Pacino, Strong has mentioned Hopkins, [Denzel Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denzel_Washington "Denzel Washington"), [Isabelle Huppert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isabelle_Huppert "Isabelle Huppert"), [Meryl Streep](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meryl_Streep "Meryl Streep"), [Philip Seymour Hoffman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_Seymour_Hoffman "Philip Seymour Hoffman"), [Ben Kingsley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Kingsley "Ben Kingsley"), [Laurence Olivier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurence_Olivier "Laurence Olivier"), [Robert Duvall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Duvall "Robert Duvall"), [Ian Holm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Holm "Ian Holm"), and [Kenneth Branagh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Branagh "Kenneth Branagh") as his influences.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-gq2019-10)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-52)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-53)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-54)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jeremy_Strong&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Personal life")]

In 2016, Strong married Emma Wall, a [Danish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark "Denmark")[psychiatrist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychiatrist "Psychiatrist") and documentary filmmaker; they met four years earlier at a party in New York City during [Hurricane Sandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Sandy "Hurricane Sandy").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-New_Yorker_profile-2) They have three daughters.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-gq2019-10)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-55)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-56)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-57)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-Guardian-211002-58) They live in New York and have homes in [Copenhagen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copenhagen "Copenhagen")[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-Guardian-211002-58)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-59) and [Tisvilde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tisvilde "Tisvilde"). Strong has said he is [not a religious](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irreligion "Irreligion") person.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Strong#cite_note-New_Yorker_profile-2)

## Awards and nominations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jeremy_Strong&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Awards and nominations")]

Main article: [List of awards and nominations received by Jeremy Strong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_awards_and_nominations_received_by_Jeremy_Strong "List of awards and nominations received by Jeremy Strong")

Strong has received [numerous accolades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_awards_and_nominations_received_by_Jeremy_Strong "List of awards and nominations received by Jeremy Strong") over his career for his roles on stage and screen. For his role as [Kendall Roy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kendall_Roy "Kendall Roy") in the [HBO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HBO "HBO") drama series _[Succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Succession\_(TV\_series) "Succession (TV series)")_ (2018–2023) he received a [Primetime Emmy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primetime_Emmy_Award_for_Outstanding_Lead_Actor_in_a_Drama_Series "Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Lead Actor in a Drama Series"), a [Golden Globe Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globe_Award_for_Best_Actor_%E2%80%93_Television_Series_Drama "Golden Globe Award for Best Actor – Television Series Drama"), and a [Critics' Choice Television Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Critics'_Choice_Television_Award_for_Best_Actor_in_a_Drama_Series "Critics' Choice Television Award for Best Actor in a Drama Series") as Best Lead Actor in a Drama Series, in addition to two [Actor Award for Outstanding Performance by an Ensemble in a Drama Series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Actor_Award_for_Outstanding_Performance_by_an_Ensemble_in_a_Drama_Series "Actor Award for Outstanding Performance by an Ensemble in a Drama Series"). For his role as Doctor Thomas Stockmann in the [Broadway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadway_(theatre) "Broadway (theatre)") revival of the [Henrik Ibsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henrik_Ibsen "Henrik Ibsen") play _[An Enemy of the People](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An\_Enemy\_of\_the\_People "An Enemy of the People")_ he received the [Tony Award for Best Leading Actor in a Play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Award_for_Best_Actor_in_a_Play "Tony Award for Best Actor in a Play"). Most recently he was nominated as Best Supporting Actor for an [Academy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Supporting_Actor "Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor"), a [BAFTA Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAFTA_Award_for_Best_Actor_in_a_Supporting_Role "BAFTA Award for Best Actor in a Supporting Role"), [Actor Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Actor_Award_for_Outstanding_Performance_by_a_Male_Actor_in_a_Supporting_Role "Actor Award for Outstanding Performance by a Male Actor in a Supporting Role") and a [Golden Globe Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globe_Award_for_Best_Supporting_Actor_%E2%80%93_Motion_Picture "Golden Globe Award for Best Supporting Actor – Motion Picture") for his role as [Roy Cohn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_Cohn "Roy Cohn") in _[The Apprentice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Apprentice\_(2024\_film) "The Apprentice (2024 film)")_.

In 2001, she made her Broadway début as Becky Thatcher in The Adventures of Tom Sawyer. She also portrayed the lead role in Pulse, a remake of a J-Horror film. In 2007, she joined the cast of Heroes playing the character Elle Bishop, and Gossip Girl as the off-screen titular narrator. In 2008, she played the title character in the comedy movie Forgetting Sarah Marshall. She has since appeared in a number of comedy films such as Fanboys, Couples Retreat, and When in Rome. Bell was also the voice of Cora in Astro Boy and is the voice and face of Lucy Stillman in the Assassin's Creed video game series. Bell has received a Satellite Award and Saturn Award, and has been nominated several times for Television Critics Association Awards and Teen Choice Awards. She is the daughter of Tom Bell, the television news director for WOAI-TV in San Antonio, and Lorelei "Lori" Bell, a registered nurse. Bell is of Polish and Scottish descent. Her parents divorced when she was two years old, and she has two half sisters, Sara and Jody, from her father's second marriage. She has four step-siblings from her mother's second marriage to John Raymond Avedian, Laura, John, Matt Avedian, and Megan. Bell has strabismus, which affects her right eye. She inherited it from her mother, who had it corrected as a child. Bell claims that if she does not get enough sleep, it aggravates the ailment. She calls her right eye "Wonky". At the age of four, Bell claimed she did not like her first name. Her mother convinced Bell to go by her middle name of Anne instead; she used the name Annie until high school. She attended Burton Elementary school in Huntington Woods. Just before her freshman year of high school, Bell's parents decided to pull her from the public school system. She then attended Shrine Catholic High School in nearby Royal Oak, where she took part in the drama and music club. During her time at the school, she won the starring role in the school's 1997 production of The Wizard of Oz as Dorothy Gale and also appeared in productions of Fiddler on the Roof (1995), Lady Be Good (1996), and Li'l Abner (1998). In 1998, the year she graduated, Bell was named the yearbook's "Best Looking Girl" by senior class vote. When Bell was 17, her best friend Jenny DeRita, whom she met at age 11 during a Detroit community theater production, was killed in an automobile accident. Bell said that it was "both the best and worst thing that has ever happened to me. [...] Once you learn not to take people for granted, you live a lot happier life". Shortly after her high school graduation, Bell moved to New York City to attend the Tisch School of the Arts at New York University, majoring in musical theater. In 2001, during her senior year at New York University, Bell left a few credits shy of graduating to take a role in the Broadway musical version of The Adventures of Tom Sawyer. Career Early work (1992–2003) In 1992, Bell went to her first audition and won a dual role as a banana and a tree in a suburban Detroit theater's production of Raggedy Ann and Andy. Her mother had established her with an agent before Bell was 13, which allowed her to appear in newspaper advertisements for several Detroit retailers and television commercials. She also began private acting lessons. In 1998, she appeared with an uncredited role in the locally filmed movie Polish Wedding. Kristen Bell also portrays Sally Wister in The History Channel’s Choosing Sides: Young Voices on the Revolution currently showing at Independence Hall visitors center in Philadelphia. In 2001, Bell left New York University to take a key role as Becky Thatcher in the short-lived Broadway musical of The Adventures of Tom Sawyer. That same year she made her credited film debut in Pootie Tang. Her one line in the film was cut and her appearance exists only as a scene shown during the credit sequence. Additionally, she auditioned for the television series Smallville for the role of Chloe Sullivan, a part eventually won by Allison Mack. In 2002, she appeared in the Broadway revival of The Crucible with Liam Neeson, Angela Bettis and Laura Linney. Bell then moved to Los Angeles, California in 2002 because of her friendship with writers Kevin Murphy and Dan Studney, and appeared in a handful of television shows as a special guest, finding trouble gaining a recurring role in a television series. Bell had "tested like eight times and booked nothing and every show [she] tested for got picked up," including auditions for Skin and a Norm Macdonald series. In 2003, she landed a role in the Hallmark Channel movie The King and Queen of Moonlight Bay. Kristen Bell appeared on the show Punk'd. Breakout (2004–2006) In 2004, Bell appeared in the Lifetime television movie Gracie's Choice, which received one of the network's highest ratings. She made her debut in a theatrically released film, with David Mamet's Spartan, as Laura Newton, the kidnapped daughter of the U.S. President, acting alongside Val Kilmer. Bell also guest-starred on the HBO's drama Deadwood in a two-episode story arc ("Bullock Returns to the Camp" and "Suffer the Little Children"). At 24 she won the role of the title character in UPN's drama Veronica Mars, which was launched in the fall of 2004. Created by Rob Thomas, the series starred Bell as the seventeen year old detective Veronica, which put her alongside actors Enrico Colantoni who played her father, Jason Dohring, Percy Daggs III and Ryan Hansen. Bell noted the parallels between the character of Veronica and her own life — Bell's parents had divorced and her best friend had also died, like that of Veronica. The series earned positive reviews from television critics, as did Bell's performance. Some critics felt that she was overlooked, however, and deserved an Emmy Award nomination. In 2005, Bell starred in Reefer Madness: The Movie Musical, reprising the role she played in the short-lived 2001 off-broadway musical. The musical was a spoof of the 1936 exploitation film of the same name. Reefer Madness: The Movie Musical debuted on the Showtime network on April 16, 2005. On September 18, 2005, Bell performed the theme song from Fame on the "Emmy Idol" portion of the 57th Annual Primetime Emmy Awards. She and the cast of Veronica Mars were nominated for two Teen Choice Awards in 2005: "Choice Breakout Actress" and "Choice Breakout TV Show". In 2006, Bell won the Saturn Award for "Best Actress on Television" for her acting on Veronica Mars, while the series was nominated for "Best Network Television Show". Aside from working on Veronica Mars, in April, Bell starred as Gracie in Fifty Pills, an entry for the Tribeca Film Festival. She appeared in a short independent film called The Receipt and the horror film Roman, which was directed by her The Crucible co-star Angela Bettis. Released on August 11, 2006, Pulse starred Bell as the lead Mattie. A remake of the Japanese horror film Kairo, the film grossed $27.9 million worldwide, however it garnered negative response from critics. Frank Scheck of The Hollywood Reporter commented, "despite the starring presence of Kristen Bell, young actress has far less interesting material to work with here than she does as [the character] "Veronica Mars."" Recent and future roles (2007–present) Veronica Mars continued on UPN until the third season, in which the show was renewed and returned on the newly created The CW. On May 17, 2007 Ostroff announced the cancellation of the series. The two-hour series finale aired in the United States on May 22, 2007, and on June 11, 2007 Thomas officially announced in an email to TV Guide's Michael Ausiello that Veronica Mars had been canceled by the CW. A Veronica Mars feature film and comic book series continuation had been discussed, and for a short time there was talk of another collaboration between Bell and creator Thomas that would be unrelated to the Veronica Mars series. Following the cancellation of Veronica Mars, Bell had voiced interest in appearing on Heroes because she was a fan previous to being cast. On July 29, 2007, during a train ride back to Los Angeles from the San Diego Comic-Con with Heroes actors Zachary Quinto and Masi Oka, and writers from the series, the writers had mentioned that if she "ever want[ed] to come on Heroes, give us [writers] a call," to which Bell said she would love to. She was also spoken to about a role on Lost, but turned down the role to portray Charlotte Staples Lewis. Announced in August 2007, Bell was to portray Elle Bishop, a "mysterious young lady" with an "awesome power". She did not have to audition for the role of Elle, who made her first appearance in an October 2007 episode, and will appear in at least thirteen episodes during the run of the series. The casting of Bell, as Heroes creator Tim Kring explains, "was not easy to pull off", but because of the large ensemble cast of the series and multiple story arcs, "we found a way to jump into a small window in Bell’s schedule." Concurrently with filming on Heroes, she narrates as title character in the CW series Gossip Girl. Shortly after the cancellation of Veronica Mars in early 2007, Bell filmed on location in Hawaii for her starring role as the title character in the Judd Apatow comedy Forgetting Sarah Marshall. She noted that the improvisational comedy in the film was "a lovely experience". The film, written by and also starring Jason Segel was released theatrically on April 18, 2008. Bell lent her voice and likeness to the video game Assassin's Creed which was released on November 13, 2007 for the PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 and April 8, 2008 for the PC. Bell reprises her role of Lucy in Assassin's Creed II released on November 17, 2009, and again in Assassin's Creed: Brotherhood, released on 16 November 2010. In the spring of 2006, she finished filming the Star Wars-themed comedy Fanboys, which had its release date pushed to January 14, 2008. This was due to additional funding given to director Kyle Newman to shoot new scenes, however, the busy schedules of the actors only allowed for filming in September 2007, thus moving the release date to accommodate that. Bell will voice the character of Marybelle in the animated feature Sheepish, which also has a 2008 release date. She also starred in the 2009 comedies Serious Moonlight, alongside Meg Ryan, and Couples Retreat, which chronicled four couples who partake in therapy sessions at a tropical island resort. Jason Bateman played her husband. On March 31, 2008, Bell began shooting for the Mark Steven Johnson-written Disney film When in Rome in locations in Rome and New York; the film was released in 2010. Bell reprised her role as Sarah Marshall for a cameo appearance in the film Get Him to the Greek, a spin-off sequel from Forgetting Sarah Marshall, released June 4, 2010. Bell has also said that when she is free from film and television roles, she would like to perform on stage again. She co-starred with singers Christina Aguilera and Cher in the movie-musical Burlesque which was released on Thanksgiving in 2010. Bell has joined the cast of Scream 4, which is set to be released on April 15, 2011. She is also attached to the films Everbody Loves Whales and Dance of the Mirlitons. She has also appeared in the music video for "Madder Red" by Brooklyn experimental rock band Yeasayer. Personal life At age 11, Bell became a vegetarian. In an interview with PETA, Bell stated, "I have always been an animal lover. I had a hard time disassociating the animals I cuddled with — dogs and cats, for example — from the animals on my plate, and I never really cared for the taste of meat. I always loved my Brussel sprouts!" During her time in Michigan, Bell fostered animals from Michigan Humane Society and she now supports the San Diego-based Helen Woodward Animal Center. Bell often attends fund raisers for the ASPCA and other non-profit organizations dedicated to protecting animals. She owns a Welsh Corgi-Chow Chow mix named Lola, a Welsh Corgi-Chihuahua mix named Shakey, and a black Labrador Retriever named Sadie, who was 11 years old when she was rescued from Hurricane Katrina and adopted by Bell in 2005. She and many of those who worked on Veronica Mars, including friend Ryan Hansen, are involved with the charity organization Invisible Children Inc. The goal of the organization is to create awareness regarding the plight of Northern Ugandans who are caught in the midst of a civil war between the government and Joseph Kony's Lord's Resistance Army. Bell has also done a public service announcement for Do Something's great Healthy Living Campaign. Bell supported, and campaigned for, Barack Obama during the 2008 presidential election. Along with Rashida Jones, she visited college campuses in Missouri to discuss the candidates and encourage voter registration. Bell has shown her support for the Writers Guild of America in the writer's strike, appearing in the picket lines in December 2007 stating, "the writers are just looking for some fairness." ## July 18, 1980 • Huntington Woods, Michigan

### Actress

By the time she was twenty-four years old, actress Kristen Bell had a resume that most seasoned performers would envy. She had starred on Broadway while still in college and had several film credits under her belt by the early 2000s. But it was thanks to the small screen and her debut as a teen supersleuth on cable channel UPN's hit drama, _Veronica Mars,_ that shot Bell from obscurity to stardom. Although the show, which premiered in September 2004, did not fare well in the ratings,it struck a chord with a core group of watchers who immediately launched hundreds of fan sites. And even the most cynical critics were wowed by the quirky new program, its interesting dialogue, and especially the smart and sassy Bell.

  

### From Detroit to New York

Kristen Bell was born on July 18, 1980, in Huntington Woods, a suburb of Detroit, Michigan, to mom, Lorelei, a registered nurse, and dad, Tom, a TV news director. Although her parents divorced when she was still a toddler, in interviews Bell recalls that her childhood was a happy one. Her father remarried when she was four years old but still remained close to his only child. Bell formed a bond with her new stepmother and two stepsisters. "I really feel close to both families," the actress revealed to Michelle Caruso in a _New York Daily News_ interview, "because I was split pretty evenly between the two."

It was apparent from early on that Bell had a talent for performing. From kindergarten through eighth grade, she attended Detroit's Burton International, a multicultural school for gifted children. She also took singing lessons and tap-dancing lessons. Bell admitted to Caruso that her initial attempts at acting were less than spectacular. When she auditioned for her first part in a community theater production of _Raggedy Ann and Andy,_ the would-be performer "flipped out" and cried. Regardless, Bell joined the cast "in the complex dual role of the banana in the first act and the tree in the second act."

While attending Shrine High School in Royal Oak, another Detroit suburb, Bell continued to sharpen her acting skills by performing with Stagecrafters, a community theater troupe based in the same city. By age fourteen, Bell even had her own agent but, as she told the _Detroit News_ , the budding actress chose to remain in metro Detroit so that she could "live like a real kid." Plus, Bell was starting to make a name for herself locally. According to her high school principal, Thomas Kirkwood, "[Kristen] was very enthusiastic, driven and entertaining. It was clear that she would be an entertainer."

Shortly before high school graduation Bell was accepted to the Tisch School of the Arts at New York University ([NYU](https://www.notablebiographies.com/knowledge/New_York_University.html "View 'nyu' definition from Wikipedia")). Her

The show is set in the upper-class, seaside town of Neptune, California, where everything is not as picture-perfect as it seems. By day she bravely stands up to the taunts of her cruel classmates with the help of her new sidekick, nerdy Wallace Fennell. By night she turns into a savvy sleuth who helps her father in his new private investigation business. Her biggest case is figuring out who really killed Lilly.

### The Original Teen Detective: Nancy Drew

[Veronica Mars](https://www.notablebiographies.com/knowledge/Veronica_Mars.html "View 'veronica mars' definition from Wikipedia") may be the new girl sleuth of the twenty-first century, but the original teen detective, Nancy Drew, is now over seventy-five years old. Although Nancy Drew originally appeared in print in 1929 she still shares many similarities with her 2005 counterpart. Like Veronica, Nancy was originally a blonde; she comes from a single-parent home; she works closely with her father, Carson Drew, a well-known attorney; and she frequently solves cases assisted by her two friends, Bess Marvin and George Fayne. More importantly, according to "The History of Nancy Drew," Nancy, like Veronica, is "the embodiment of independence, pluck, and intelligence."

Nancy Drew was the product of American author [Edward Stratemeyer](https://www.notablebiographies.com/knowledge/Edward_Stratemeyer.html "View 'edward stratemeyer' definition from Wikipedia") (1862–1930) and his Edward Stratemeyer Syndicate, a writing company that churned out popular series for young people. Favorite characters, such as the Rover Boys, Tom Swift, and the Bobbsey Twins, appeared in book after book, and eventually became literary heroes. Because readers gobbled up the stories, and Stratemeyer could not possibly keep up with the demand, he hired a crew of ghostwriters (authors whose work is credited to someone else) who fleshed out his original outlines.

Young female heroines were featured in previous Stratemeyer series, but they were usually fairly traditional. With the introduction of Nancy Drew, a new kind of independent woman was born. The credit is given primarily to Mildred A. Wort Benson (1905–2002), who wrote twenty-three of the original thirty Nancy Drew stories. (Although the name "[Carolyn Keene](https://www.notablebiographies.com/knowledge/Carolyn_Keene.html "View 'carolyn keene' definition from Wikipedia")" appears on the book covers, it was simply the pen name [alias] shared by the many writers the Nancy Drew series had over the years.) According to "The History of Nancy Drew," Benson was tired of what she called the "namby-pamby style of girls' series books, and she had no intention of characterizing Nancy as namby-pamby." The feisty ghostwriter believed that girls could do anything boys could do, and she instilled that same feistiness in her character.

Benson was twenty-four when she wrote the very first Nancy Drew mystery in 1929, _The Secret of the Old Clock,_ and she continued to breathe life into her favorite girl detective for the next thirty years. When she quit the syndicate in 1959, Edward Stratemeyer's daughter, Harriet, took up the pen and wrote the majority of the original series, which consists of 175 books. The early Nancy Drew mysteries are still being reissued by Simon … Schuster, which purchased the Stratemeyer Syndicate in 1984. The company also produces a modern-day version of the series called _Nancy Drew: Girl Detective,_ as well as other spin-off series, including _The Nancy Drew Notebooks_ and _The Nancy Drew Files._

## July 18, 1980 • Huntington Woods, Michigan

### Actress

By the time she was twenty-four years old, actress Kristen Bell had a resume that most seasoned performers would envy. She had starred on Broadway while still in college and had several film credits under her belt by the early 2000s. But it was thanks to the small screen and her debut as a teen supersleuth on cable channel UPN's hit drama, _Veronica Mars,_ that shot Bell from obscurity to stardom. Although the show, which premiered in September 2004, did not fare well in the ratings,it struck a chord with a core group of watchers who immediately launched hundreds of fan sites. And even the most cynical critics were wowed by the quirky new program, its interesting dialogue, and especially the smart and sassy Bell.

  

### From Detroit to New York

Kristen Bell was born on July 18, 1980, in Huntington Woods, a suburb of Detroit, Michigan, to mom, Lorelei, a registered nurse, and dad, Tom, a TV news director. Although her parents divorced when she was still a toddler, in interviews Bell recalls that her childhood was a happy one. Her father remarried when she was four years old but still remained close to his only child. Bell formed a bond with her new stepmother and two stepsisters. "I really feel close to both families," the actress revealed to Michelle Caruso in a _New York Daily News_ interview, "because I was split pretty evenly between the two."

It was apparent from early on that Bell had a talent for performing. From kindergarten through eighth grade, she attended Detroit's Burton International, a multicultural school for gifted children. She also took singing lessons and tap-dancing lessons. Bell admitted to Caruso that her initial attempts at acting were less than spectacular. When she auditioned for her first part in a community theater production of _Raggedy Ann and Andy,_ the would-be performer "flipped out" and cried. Regardless, Bell joined the cast "in the complex dual role of the banana in the first act and the tree in the second act."

While attending Shrine High School in Royal Oak, another Detroit suburb, Bell continued to sharpen her acting skills by performing with Stagecrafters, a community theater troupe based in the same city. By age fourteen, Bell even had her own agent but, as she told the _Detroit News_ , the budding actress chose to remain in metro Detroit so that she could "live like a real kid." Plus, Bell was starting to make a name for herself locally. According to her high school principal, Thomas Kirkwood, "[Kristen] was very enthusiastic, driven and entertaining. It was clear that she would be an entertainer."

Shortly before high school graduation Bell was accepted to the Tisch School of the Arts at New York University ([NYU](https://www.notablebiographies.com/knowledge/New_York_University.html "View 'nyu' definition from Wikipedia")). Her

Bell also began 2004 with a recurring role as Flora Anderson in HBO's wild west drama, _Deadwood._ Bell's next leap was to the big screen, where she appeared in the thriller _Spartan,_ written and directed by legendary American playwright [David Mamet](https://www.notablebiographies.com/knowledge/David_Mamet.html "View 'david mamet' definition from Wikipedia") (1947–). Although her role as Laura Newton, the kidnapped daughter of the president of the United States, was relatively small, it brought Bell a good deal of exposure. In fact, the film drew the attention of producer and writer Rob Thomas (1965–), who was casting a new television series called _Veronica Mars._

Bell, however, was not a clear choice for the role of the lively seventeen-year-old detective. When Thomas created the series, he had not envisioned a five-foot-two, perky blonde with a sunny smile. Instead, he thought much darker. According to Bell, who spoke with Craig Byrne's _NeptuneSite,_ Thomas describes _Veronica_ as a cross between _Twin Peaks,_ an edgy drama from the early 1990s, and _Dawson's Creek,_ the teen soap opera that Thomas wrote for in the late 1990s. Regardless of her blonde, girl-next-door looks, Bell beat out seventy other hopefuls and won the part of the teen sleuth who is wise beyond her years. And Thomas was glad he cast her. As he told Jennifer Armstrong, "Without Bell, _Veronica_ wouldn't be the wry delight that it is."

The show is set in the upper-class, seaside town of Neptune, California, where everything is not as picture-perfect as it seems. Veronica's best friend, Lilly Kane, is killed, and her sheriff dad, Keith Mars, accuses Lilly's powerful tycoon father of being the killer. Veronica's world is shattered. Her mother abandons the family, and Veronica, once one of the most popular girls at school, is suddenly an outcast. By day she bravely stands up to the taunts of her cruel classmates with the help of her new sidekick, nerdy Wallace Fennell. By night she turns into a savvy sleuth who helps her father in his new private investigation business. Her biggest case is figuring out who really killed Lilly.

When _Veronica Mars_ debuted on September 22, 2004, critics went wild and heaped praise on Thomas for his intricate plot twists and clever characters. Barry Garron of the _Hollywood Reporter_ called it "one of TV's only bright spots." He further enthused that the show "has comedy, deathly serious drama, parody and danger, ingredients not typically mixed together. The result is a new TV flavor, and it's delicious." The press was especially kind to newcomer Bell. According to _Variety's_ Phil Gallo, Bell "gives a multilayered performance, and is as charismatic as she is tough and intelligent." After only a few episodes, Kristen Bell was a huge hit on television.

### The Original Teen Detective: Nancy Drew

[Veronica Mars](https://www.notablebiographies.com/knowledge/Veronica_Mars.html "View 'veronica mars' definition from Wikipedia") may be the new girl sleuth of the twenty-first century, but the original teen detective, Nancy Drew, is now over seventy-five years old. Although Nancy Drew originally appeared in print in 1929 she still shares many similarities with her 2005 counterpart. Like Veronica, Nancy was originally a blonde; she comes from a single-parent home; she works closely with her father, Carson Drew, a well-known attorney; and she frequently solves cases assisted by her two friends, Bess Marvin and George Fayne. More importantly, according to "The History of Nancy Drew," Nancy, like Veronica, is "the embodiment of independence, pluck, and intelligence."

Nancy Drew was the product of American author [Edward Stratemeyer](https://www.notablebiographies.com/knowledge/Edward_Stratemeyer.html "View 'edward stratemeyer' definition from Wikipedia") (1862–1930) and his Edward Stratemeyer Syndicate, a writing company that churned out popular series for young people. Favorite characters, such as the Rover Boys, Tom Swift, and the Bobbsey Twins, appeared in book after book, and eventually became literary heroes. Because readers gobbled up the stories, and Stratemeyer could not possibly keep up with the demand, he hired a crew of ghostwriters (authors whose work is credited to someone else) who fleshed out his original outlines.

Young female heroines were featured in previous Stratemeyer series, but they were usually fairly traditional. With the introduction of Nancy Drew, a new kind of independent woman was born. The credit is given primarily to Mildred A. Wort Benson (1905–2002), who wrote twenty-three of the original thirty Nancy Drew stories. (Although the name "[Carolyn Keene](https://www.notablebiographies.com/knowledge/Carolyn_Keene.html "View 'carolyn keene' definition from Wikipedia")" appears on the book covers, it was simply the pen name [alias] shared by the many writers the Nancy Drew series had over the years.) According to "The History of Nancy Drew," Benson was tired of what she called the "namby-pamby style of girls' series books, and she had no intention of characterizing Nancy as namby-pamby." The feisty ghostwriter believed that girls could do anything boys could do, and she instilled that same feistiness in her character.

Benson was twenty-four when she wrote the very first Nancy Drew mystery in 1929, _The Secret of the Old Clock,_ and she continued to breathe life into her favorite girl detective for the next thirty years. When she quit the syndicate in 1959, Edward Stratemeyer's daughter, Harriet, took up the pen and wrote the majority of the original series, which consists of 175 books. The early Nancy Drew mysteries are still being reissued by Simon … Schuster, which purchased the Stratemeyer Syndicate in 1984. The company also produces a modern-day version of the series called _Nancy Drew: Girl Detective,_ as well as other spin-off series, including _The Nancy Drew Notebooks_ and _The Nancy Drew Files._
